column2: Positional pain with saddle ST elevation and previous TB with calcified hilar nodes suggests tuberculous pericarditis; echo and fluid ADA/culture.
Point tenderness and crepitus after a fall are rib fractures, here complicated by a small traumatic pneumothorax; analgesia and assess size.
ST elevation in V4–V6 with markedly raised troponin is an anterolateral STEMI; diabetics often have atypical pain. Reperfuse if < 12 h.
Ischaemic pain with a non-diagnostic ECG: high-sensitivity troponin at presentation and at 1–3 h to diagnose or exclude NSTEMI.
Exertional syncope, jerky pulse, murmur louder on Valsalva and familial sudden death suggest HCM; transthoracic echo is the key test.
Exertional angina in a smoker: exercise testing is the best listed option, though NICE/ESC now prefer CT coronary angiography first.
Prolonged fever, weight loss and a murmur in congenital heart disease is IE: ≥ 3 blood culture sets before antibiotics.
Fixed S2 splitting with a flow murmur but normal TTE suggests an ASD missed by TTE (e.g. sinus venosus); TOE or cardiac MRI.
Sudden chest tightness and hypotension after surgery is PE until proven otherwise: CTPA (bedside echo if too unstable).
ST elevation in II, III, aVF with reciprocal I/aVL depression is inferior STEMI (RCA); record V4R and avoid nitrates if RV involved.
ST elevation V1–V4 with evolving Q waves is anterior STEMI (LAD), the worst-prognosis territory: primary PCI.
ST elevation in I, aVL, V5–V6 with reciprocal inferior depression is lateral STEMI (circumflex or diagonal).
Widespread concave ST elevation with PR depression after a viral illness is acute pericarditis: NSAID plus colchicine.
Early-morning rest pain with transient ST elevation, normal troponin and normal coronaries is Prinzmetal angina: CCB and nitrates.
Persistent ST elevation with Q waves 8 weeks after anterior MI with heart failure suggests LV aneurysm; echo confirms.
Continuous machinery murmur below the left clavicle with bounding pulses and chest infections is PDA; device or surgical closure.
Chest pain, ST elevation, raised troponin and new anterior akinesia is acute STEMI: primary PCI, then ACEi and beta-blocker.
Rheumatic history with congestion, preserved LV function, AF, tapping apex and diastolic rumble is MS with AF: warfarin.
New heart failure at 8 months' pregnancy without another cause is peripartum cardiomyopathy (EF < 45%).
Recurrent syncope with a slow-rising pulse, narrow pulse pressure and aortic ejection murmur is severe AS: valve replacement.
Recurrent symptomatic complete heart block after inferior MI unresponsive to atropine needs temporary transvenous pacing.
Hypotension, pulsus paradoxus, raised JVP and electrical alternans is tamponade: urgent echo-guided pericardiocentesis.
Stable regular narrow-complex tachycardia after failed vagal manoeuvres: IV adenosine 6, 12, then 18 mg.
Recent AF with pulmonary oedema and hypotension is unstable: synchronised DC cardioversion under sedation.
Frequent unifocal ectopics in an asymptomatic man with a normal heart are benign: reassure and cut caffeine and alcohol.
Non-massive PE (hypoxaemic, normotensive) on the pill: oxygen and therapeutic LMWH; thrombolysis only if haemodynamically compromised.
Weakness after diarrhoea with ST depression, flat T and U waves is hypokalaemia: replace K⁺ (and Mg) with monitoring.
Chaotic waveforms without QRS in a pulseless patient is VF: immediate defibrillation and CPR.
Polymorphic VT with twisting axis on QT-prolonging drugs is torsades: IV magnesium 2 g and stop the drugs.
Paroxysmal AF needing rhythm control with CHA2DS2-VASc 4: an antiarrhythmic (sotalol) plus anticoagulation (DOAC preferred).
A long sinus pause coinciding with syncope and no reversible cause is sinus node dysfunction: permanent pacemaker.
Symptomatic benign unifocal ventricular ectopics despite reassurance and no caffeine: a beta-blocker is first line.
Stable regular narrow-complex SVT after failed modified Valsalva: IV adenosine with ECG recording.
Apical pansystolic murmur to the axilla with S3 is significant mitral regurgitation.
Mid-systolic click then late systolic murmur at the apex is mitral valve prolapse.
An apical mid-diastolic rumble with a collapsing pulse and early diastolic murmur is the Austin Flint murmur of severe AR.
Pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge louder on inspiration (Carvallo) is tricuspid regurgitation.
Irregularly irregular narrow complexes without P waves is AF; assess CHA2DS2-VASc and choose rate or rhythm control.
Broad QRS with QS in V1–V3, discordant ST changes and left axis is old LBBB; echo for structural disease (new LBBB with pain = STEMI equivalent).
Inferior STEMI with ST elevation in V4R, hypotension and clear lungs is RV infarction: fluids, no nitrates, primary PCI.
Progressive PR lengthening until a dropped beat with grouped beating is Mobitz I (Wenckebach), benign in athletes.
Brief faint with pallor on prolonged standing in a warm place, rapid recovery and normal ECG is vasovagal syncope.
A slurred QRS upstroke (delta wave) with short PR is WPW; AF conducting down the pathway can cause VF and collapse. Ablate.
Collapse with AF and new left hemiparesis is a right-hemisphere stroke (cardioembolic): urgent CT before thrombolysis/thrombectomy.
Postural syncope soon after starting an antihypertensive (e.g. doxazosin) is first-dose hypotension; start low at bedtime.
SpO2 < 92% is a life-threatening feature: oxygen, nebulised salbutamol + ipratropium, steroids and IV magnesium 1.2–2 g, with early ICU review.
Acute severe asthma (PEF 33–50%, no life-threatening feature): repeated nebulised salbutamol, oxygen to 94–98% and prednisolone 40–50 mg.
COPD exacerbation with acidosis: controlled O2 (88–92%), nebulised salbutamol/ipratropium, prednisolone, antibiotic; NIV if acidosis persists.
LTOT (≥ 15 h/day) for stable PaO2 < 7.3 kPa, or 7.3–8 with oedema, polycythaemia or pulmonary hypertension; it improves survival.
Wheeze comes from narrowed airways (asthma, bronchitis, foreign body). Pneumothorax gives reduced breath sounds and hyper-resonance, not wheeze.
Smoking cessation and LTOT (for chronic hypoxaemia) are the classic interventions that prolong survival in COPD.
DLCO is low in emphysema (alveolar destruction) but near normal in chronic bronchitis; spirometry is obstructive in both.
SpO2 < 92% is life-threatening asthma (with PEF < 33%, silent chest, normal PaCO2, exhaustion); PEF 33–50% is acute severe.
Childhood asthma is commoner in boys, but after puberty it is commoner and more severe in women.
In hypercapnic COPD with PaO2 8.2 kPa (SpO2 ~90%), 35% oxygen would worsen CO2 retention; use 24–28% Venturi to SpO2 88–92%.
Ventilate in asthma for exhaustion, drowsiness, confusion, arrest or rising PaCO2 despite maximal therapy; involve ICU early.
CXR signs of COPD correlate poorly with airflow limitation, which is graded by post-bronchodilator FEV1 (GOLD 1–4).
Long-acting bronchodilators (LAMA + LABA) are maintenance in moderate–severe COPD; short-acting agents are relievers only.
Uncontrolled asthma on low-dose ICS + SABA: switch to low-dose ICS–formoterol MART (BTS/NICE/SIGN 2024, GINA). Never LABA without ICS.
Post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC < 0.70 in a symptomatic smoker confirms COPD; partial reversibility does not exclude it.
